title: Pittsburgh Penguins V. Nashville Predators Preview: Lineups, Where To Watch - Yahoo Sports
content: After snapping a four-game skid on Thursday in a commanding 4-0 win over the Florida Panthers, the Pittsburgh Penguins will look to build on that when they take on the Nashville Predators Saturday at PPG Paints Arena in Pittsburgh. The Penguins played a full 60 minutes Thursday, getting contributions from up and down their new-look lineup. They were without the services of forwards Bryan Rust and Ben Kindel - who were both placed on injured reserve Thursday - and it appears they will be without another forward Saturday. Forward Evgeni Malkin, who missed Friday's team practice with an illness and who registered a goal and two points in Thursday's win, was ruled out by Penguins' head coach Dan Muse after the morning skate, which Malkin participated in. Forward Egor Chinakhov, who is day-to-day with an undisclosed injury, is expected to miss his second consecutive game. In addition, defenseman Sam Girard was officially placed on injured reserve with an upper-body injury, and the Penguins recalled forward Avery Hayes from Wilkes-Barre/Scranton (WBS) to fill Malkin's hole in the lineup. Goaltender Arturs Silovs - who posted a 25-save shutout Thursday - will get his second consecutive nod in goal Saturday. There were no line rushes during the Penguins' optional morning skate, and it is difficult to tell where Hayes will fit into a lineup that was already shorthanded to a pretty large degree. He has had some legitimate chemistry with Rutger McGroarty in WBS, and both had nine points in six AHL games, so it won't come as a surprise if they begin the game on the same line. Takeaways: Penguins Deliver Near-Perfect 60-Minute Effort In 4-0 Win Over Panthers To Snap Four-Game Losing StreakAfter a disastrous, winless four-game Western road trip, the Penguins put together their best effort of the season Thursday against Florida. title: USC v Wisconsin live updates: Score, highlights, predictions, analysis - Yahoo Sports
content: USC football, after a week off, went to Madison to face the Wisconsin Badgers. The Trojans knew they couldn't get caught looking ahead to Ohio State. Based on how they played in a very ugly first half, maybe some of the guys are thinking about the Buckeyes and not the Badgers. USC trails 10-7 after Jayden Maiava threw two interceptions and Jontez Williams committed a brutal pass interference penalty which enabled Wisconsin to take the lead with under two minutes left before halftime. The Trojans' offensive line has been outplayed by Wisconsin's defensive line. USC can't run the ball consistently. After a week off, this was certainly not what the coaching staff hoped to see. Wisconsin's offense needs help. USC, in the first half, helped that offense by giving it a great drive start to set up a field goal, and then committing the penalty to turn three into seven. That's exactly how USC will get defeated. It's up to the Trojans to be a lot better after halftime. Get real-time updates, turning points, and analysis for the second half of USC's game against Wisconsin. Follow along: Hit refresh for the latest updates from USC football's Week 8 game against Wisconsin at Camp Randall Stadium. This is Year 5 of the Lincoln Riley era at USC, and this stuff is still happening. We're done here, and hopefully Lincoln Riley will soon be done in Los Angeles. He needs to be. Seven points in 47 minutes. Two missed field goals. This, after a week off. Lincoln Riley's USC tenure is slipping away. The Trojans and Lincoln Riley have 15 minutes to save their season. What kind of response will we see from a team which has been thoroughly outplayed for three quarters? Now special teams joins the parade of mistakes. This is all going downhill, and Lincoln Riley is on the verge of losing the kind of game he has lost far too many times at USC. #USC OL Hayden Treter down on the field and screaming in pain.Teammates immediately call for the trainers. Appeared to be looking at hos left knee or left ankle. USC's defense starts the second half by committing a late-hit penalty and overrunning gaps, then getting outflanked on a 4th and 2 play which goes for a touchdown. Other than that, how was the play, Mrs. Lincoln? The Trojans had a week off to get healthy and become a sharper, tougher, better team. In the first half, the Trojans did not look the part. That was a very poor performance. They better come out roaring in the second half. USC takes the lead, so what do the Trojans do? They allow a very long touchdown drive featuring a terrible pass interference penalty by Jontez Williams, who grabbed Wisconsin's tight end on a pass which sailed out of the end zone. A defensive back has to force the pass catcher to make a play on a bad pass. Instead, Wisconsin - which faced second and long after a holding penalty created by Jahkeem Stewart - gets seven and the lead. The Trojans do cash in the penalty for seven, but the running game got stuffed twice before Maiava threw a touchdown pass on 3rd and goal from the 2. The Trojans need to make improvements on the ground, even though they did take the lead. In a poorly-played game, it's the Badgers' turn to do something dumb. You rarely see a face-mask penalty in pass coverage on 3rd and goal, but that's what Wisconsin just did. USC first and goal inside the 2. On a day in the Big Ten which has featured horrible offense, USC and Wisconsin are joining the parade. The Trojans are very lucky Wisconsin's offense isn't very competent. Otherwise, this could be 10-0 or 14-0. USC is fortunate to be down only three. The Trojans have to be able to run block if they want to develop a complete offense and take the next step in their evolution on that side of the ball. Weirdly but genuinely, the defense might be USC's better side of the ball in this game, if only because Wisconsin is so bad on offense and so thoroughly solid on defense. The Wisconsin offense is so bad that it is making USC's defense look good. Credit to the Trojans for doing what they are supposed to do, but the Badgers don't have a lot to offer on offense. It reinforces how winnable this game is for USC, if the Trojans can simply stop making bad mistakes. Maiava needs to be a rock for USC. Again, Wisconsin's offense isn't likely to score on its own. It will need help. Maiava had no one open on third down. He needs to throw the ball away and live to play another possession. Punt the ball and pin this bad Wisconsin offense deep. Jayden Maiava needed to protect the ball, since Wisconsin's offense likely needed help to score points. Sure enough, he throws an interception. At least the defense held the Badgers to three instead of allowing seven. USC goes three and out. Then the Trojans get two sacks to stop Wisconsin on its first possession. This game did not feel like a shootout going in, and the first two possessions did not change that view. FINAL INJURY REPORT: #USC's TE Mark Bowman and DL Jide Abasiri are moved to GAME-TIME DECISIONS @On3USC pic.twitter.com/26usScDh3E USC 24, Wisconsin 17. Wisconsin just doesn't have enough of an offense to threaten the vulnerable USC defense. As long as USC doesn't commit turnovers or do other things (allowing a blocked punt) to give Wisconsin's offense very favorable drive start positions, the Trojans should win ... but it won't be easy, and of course, there's no guarantee USC will avoid mistakes the way it did at Penn State. title: Leinster v Munster: Five takeaways as 'self-inflicted wound' and two 'ridiculous pieces of skill' cost visitors who led for 56 minutes - Planet Rugby
content: Leinster celebrate Tommy O'Brien's first-half try and, inset, Munster No.10 Charlie O'Shea After a deserved 24-18 bonus-point win for Leinster against Munster in Saturday’s United Rugby Championship round four fixture, Planet Rugby picks out five takeaways from the Irish derby. Munster lit up last season’s early URC exchanges with an ambush win at Croke Park 12 months ago, and their brand of lightning very nearly struck again across the capital city at the Aviva Stadium, where they led for 56 minutes before wilting to Leinster’s stubbornness. With Storm Boelo knocking about on a full moon evening, Munster got the scoreboard moving with a seventh-minute Charlie O’Shea penalty kick after James Ryan had tackled too high. Keenly fought exchanges followed before the visitors’ greater enthusiasm and better accuracy at the breakdown told. It was a 27th-minute gallop from Sean O’Brien into open country that shattered the home defence, and the supporting Craig Casey then handled to allow Shane Daly to make it to the line for the converted score despite Hugo Keenan’s despairing tackle. A monster O’Shea penalty kick from halfway soon followed after Joey Carbery became illegally tangled up at the breakdown, and it was only then that Leinster finally responded, eating into the 13-0 score with a glorious Jamison Gibson-Park pass getting Tommy O’Brien in out wide for a 34th-minute unconverted try. The eight-point gap was eventually eaten into after a second-half period of pressure was ignited with a correctly reversed penalty incident involving Ronan Kelleher. It ended with five-metre scrum penalties resulting in Ryan Baird’s 54th-minute converted try. A yellow card was also shown to Alex Nankivell, making it a double-whammy concession for Munster. Leinster then profited from this man-up situation, a fluffed Tadhg Beirne lineout catch resulting in the pressure that culminated in Charlie Tector’s 63rd-minute lead-taking unconverted try. At only 17-13 down, there was still hope that Munster could muster a response but with their momentum gone, it was Leinster who finished things off with their bonus point try, Gibson-Park firing off another worldie of a pass to enable Jamie Osborne to grab the 73rd-minute score. To their credit, Clayton McMillan’s side did grab a losing bonus point with Ben O’Connor’s 82nd-minute try, but the visitors trooped off with regret that a winning position wasn’t better protected. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. Last Wednesday’s latest Ireland squad announcement suggested that McMillan wouldn’t have to open his mouth to fire up his Munster team for this URC derby. Seventeen Leinster picks and just two from Munster was a new low in the different Test-level fortunes of these provinces, with further pain inflicted by the inclusion of nine players from Ulster and eight from Connacht, two teams that Munster consistently finish above every season in the league. Their fury delivered a warm response, Munster securing a healthy 13-point lead but despite generating breakdown nuisance in the guise of Gavin Coombes and possessing tackle-their-hearts-out contributors in the form of Marcus van der Merwe and Alex Kendellen, they ran out of gas in the second half. New signing Kieran Brookes didn’t cover himself in glory. Instead of Munster potentially having a penalty kick for a 16-5 lead, the TMO discovered he had pushed Kelleher off the ball, resulting in the penalty reversal, where insult was then added by back-to-back scrum penalties before Baird’s try. It was in this window that Munster suffered the self-inflicted wound that was the beginning of the end for them, but they also found the passing of Gibson-Park unstoppable. The Leinster No.9’s two try assists were ridiculous pieces of skill and that quality was decisive even though just six points separated the teams at the finish. Munster weren’t helped by their indiscipline, the penalty count going 17-11 against them with a yellow card also thrown into the mix after an opening half where their level of grit was seen in the generous number of turnovers that came their way. Leinster player ratings: ‘Mind-boggling’ Jamison Gibson-Park masterminds Munster’s demise while Andrew Porter overcomes ‘pancake’ There is an adage in rugby to let specialist position players play those specialist positions so that you play to your strengths, but Leinster decided to gamble with this premise by positioning Dan Sheehan at No.8 rather than at hooker, where he is viewed as world-class. It was last April when the positional switch first happened, with Leo Cullen making a mid-game tactical change in the Champions Cup quarter-final win over Sale, but amid injuries and an absence of faith in Max Deegan, the head coach opted to give the hooker a first-time start at No.8. The winners will claim that the experiment was a real success. After all, the post-game stats credited the skipper with a chart-topping 17 carries and a 60-metre gain, but the ruse wasn’t that easy on the eye at times. It was at a 20th-minute scrum when we first got to see him attack at No.8. Some metres were made before he was tackled outside the 22, but Munster’s Coombes was the more effective eight in the opening half. It was only when Leinster were invited to take control from about the 50th minute onwards did we get to see better Sheehan involvements, although he won’t want to recall the 61st minute incident that was getting penalised with the poaching Beirne all over him. He remained in the back row after Kelleher was replaced by sub hooker Gus McCarthy, who soon misplaced a lineout throw from five metres out that could have been costly before Leinster eventually claimed their bonus. Leinster v Munster: Winners and losers as visitors put bodies on the line but ill-discipline proves to be their undoing The Joey versus Charlie head-to-head at No.10 was a fun watch on a cold night. It’s incredible to think a decade had passed since a fresh-faced Carbery lit up Leinster in Cullen’s second season in charge. There we were, though, watching the 30-year-old on this stormy Saturday, making his first start back at the club he exited for Munster in 2018, a bold switch that unfortunately never worked out due to a rotten run with injury. Jack Crowley eventually became Munster’s go-to 10 but with McMillan’s fancy sidelined (there must be something ick in the Munster waters), the baton passed to 20-year-old rookie O’Shea ahead of the benched JJ Hanrahan and a lovely contest brewed up between the pair. O’Shea had the better of the early exchanges, varying the play and demonstrating he was more reliable off the kicking tee than his older adversary – that long-range first-half penalty was a peach, highlighting how huge his confidence was after he slipped a slick short pass to get O’Brien through the hole for Munster’s opening try. Experience, however, eventually held sway. A younger Carbery might have wilted in the frustration of seeing an accuracy-lacking Leinster struggle, as they did in the opening half, but he had the composure to become the more influential 10 when the contest turned in the second period. The cheer received when he went off near the finish was deserved, but O’Shea deserves plenty of kudos for the part he played. Munster player ratings: Ireland star’s ‘excellent all-round effort’ not good enough in defeat against Leinster Rugby tickets have become a talking point in Ireland with the national team struggling to get overpriced seats sold for their brutally timed kick-offs versus Argentina and Fiji. Thankfully, this URC derby offered better value for money and a healthy bank holiday weekend attendance turned up despite the weather and the reduced level of train services. Understandably, the majority of fans were backing blue as it was a Leinster home game. But the Irish rivalry was set aside in the eighth minute when the crowd united in a minute-long applause to commemorate 10 years since the tragic passing of Anthony Foley. A picture of the former Munster coach from his playing days was put up on the two stadium screens, and the applause lasted a full 60 seconds while play continued on the pitch. It was a lovely serious moment, and it was apt that it took place at a time when Foley’s old side were 3-0 up. Less serious was the crowd hilarity that greeted referee Andrew Brace getting sucked into a play-stopping 32nd-minute breakdown. The official was caught in the wrong place as Sheehan came around the corner and he ended up going off his feet, feeling the impact of the collision and a scrum being needed to restart play. title: Kawasaki's 50-HP Cruiser Outsizes The Honda Rebel 500 And Yamaha V Star 250 - HotCars
content: When you picture a traditional cruiser motorcycle, the image in your mind is rarely small or subtle. More often than not, the emphasis is on plenty of road presence with a long, low stance, a wide rear tire, a broad fuel tank, and real physical heft. That imposing stature usually comes with a price tag to match, sometimes close to the cost of a decent used car. But Kawasaki’s 50-horsepower underdog defies that logic, delivering a bigger footprint than its price suggests. As a general rule of thumb, the bigger and more imposing a cruiser becomes, the faster its price tends to climb. Before long, you're looking at motorcycles that cost $15,000 or more before accessories even come into the picture. On the other hand, settling for affordable machines that follow a familiar formula usually means compact dimensions and a tighter saddle. So, the answer lies in a value middle ground that refuses to compromise on physical presence without draining your bank account. After all, what gives the true stature is not necessarily the highest V-twin power and its rumble. Instead, the appeal comes from a commanding road presence, substantial proportions, plenty of chrome, and an oozing timeless silhouette. More importantly, it should feel planted on the highway and deliver oodles of low-end grunt. Bringing that exact middle ground of full-size cruiser proportions at a middleweight price is the Kawasaki Vulcan 900 Classic. The package includes a long-wheelbase frame, one of the largest rear tires in its class, and a massive fuel tank, delivering strong road presence. It also comes with a proven V-twin motor that pumps out a smooth 50 horsepower and the relaxed highway stability of a heavier big twin. Moreover, you get three different variants: the traditional-styled Classic trim, the drag-styled Custom trim, and the touring-oriented Classic LT trim. The Vulcan 900 Classic starts at $9,599, undercutting both Harley-Davidson’s Nightster and Indian’s Scout models by $400. Of course, it is not a beginner Harley alternative. Instead, its full-size look pits it against the Street Bob and the Chief, both listed at $14,999. That means a massive gap of $5,400, which stretches to $6,400 when stacked against the Sportster S. Because of that, the Kawasaki makes for a compelling, value-packed package among the heavyweight V-twin contenders in the market. Unlike larger big-bore V-twins, the Vulcan 900 Classic uses a bulletproof 903cc liquid-cooled 55-degree V-twin that has been doing duty since the 2009 update. This proven powertrain features an 88 mm bore and a 74.2 mm stroke with a lower 9.5:1 compression ratio, tuned for usable, everyday performance rather than a top-end rush. In addition, fuel injection with dual 34mm throttle bodies and sub-throttle valves helps keep throttle response crisp in different conditions. Now for the honest part. The V-twin engine makes 51 horsepower at 5,500 rpm and 58.2 pound-feet of torque at a low 3,500 rpm. That puts it at approachable power figures. However, the pull arrives low in the rev range. Better yet, it is enough to hold highway speeds with stability, so the bike never feels out of its depth on the interstate. Moreover, paired with a five-speed manual gearbox and a Kevlar-reinforced belt final drive, power flows smoothly and quietly to the rear wheel. Size is where the Vulcan 900 Classic earns its keep over smaller starter cruisers. It's easy to see why. Built around a double-cradle frame, it features a long 64.8-inch wheelbase that stretches beyond the likes of the Rebel 500 and V Star 250, sitting at 58.7 inches. As a result, Vulcan offers a substantial 97 inches of length and tips the scale at a hefty 619.6 pounds wet, providing rock-solid highway tracking. Even so, at just 26.8-inch seat height, the Kawasaki keeps the saddle lower than both smaller bikes, keeping your feet closer to the ground at stops. Furthermore, to keep its old-school lines and everyday comfort, Kawasaki tucked a Uni-Trak rear shock out of sight under a hardtail-style profile. It offers seven-way preload adjustment and 4.1 inches of travel. Up front, a 41mm Showa telescopic fork provides 5.9 inches of travel. Braking comes from a single 300mm front disc and a single 270mm rear disc, each using twin-piston calipers. Finally, the whole package rolls on a 16/15-inch wheel setup, with that wide 180 mm rear tire adding to the muscular stance. Since its launch, Kawasaki has barely made visual changes to the Vulcan 900 Classic. Its timeless American-style design nails a classic hardtail old-school vibe, a low-slung stance, wide pullback handlebars, sweeping valanced fenders, dual chrome exhaust, and chrome accents. Then, supporting the comfortable riding stance are rider floorboards and a heel-toe shifter. Meanwhile, tank-mounted round instrumentation packs an analog speedometer and small LCD screen that continues the vintage theme. Backing up that stylish presence is a legendary track record of Japanese durability, with owners routinely clocking thousands of miles with just simple maintenance. In addition, low long-term upkeep costs further boost its value along with hassle-free ownership. Overall, the Vulcan 900 Classic is the underrated cruiser that bridges the gap between compact options and overpriced big-twins. That's because the story here is no horsepower numbers. Rather, it's about full-scale size, traditional proportions, and value quotient. We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. title: Gasperini reflects on Napoli v Roma - AS Roma
content:
The team played their own game and never stopped. Our substitutions made the difference. There are many positives that come to mind, but their spirit is what really shows how mature this group is. “Yes, except for the first thirty minutes: in that phase, Napoli outperformed us, we struggled in our build-up play and in creating something. After that, we played a good final part of the first half. Then there was the second half. We had many chances and believed we could win. Napoli’s third goal could have been the end for us, but we managed to score the equaliser, with a lot of energy and belief.” You showed a lot of character, because you never lost control. You remained sharp, with ideas, and stayed patient. “That’s true. We did well in that respect, without getting frantic, by maintaining positional discipline and preserving our playing style. We were pushing up effectively with several players; those who came off the bench brought a lot of energy. [Matias] Soule did great, as did others. We’re in a great place right now. We’re confident, we’re playing good football and are trying to keep this up, and our morale is high. We feel like we’ve dropped two points, but this outcome is also good.” This is Roma’s third draw, following Inter and Como. What is most satisfying to you about these draws? “They are three different draws, but in all three games we felt we were competitive. We could’ve won against Inter, while against Como we had to play the second half down to ten men. I need more time to reflect on today’s game. However, we must recognise Napoli’s quality: they are a very good team. They’ve won the league title twice. They are a very good, experienced team. If you take on a team like them with this energy and determination, you can take on many other teams too, with the feeling that you can be competitive.” Leonardo Balerdi scored a brace. He’s got a lot of character. “I said it at the start of the season about Balerdi and [Marten] De Roon: these two players were leaders in their previous teams, two captains, and they settled in immediately. Over these past few weeks, their contribution has been extraordinary and settling into the team has been very easy for them. I’m very happy that Balerdi scored a brace; he’s a major asset to the team.” © 2018-2026 A.S. Roma S.r.l. – EU VAT IT01180281006 - all rights reserved. title: Leicester player ratings v Northampton: 'Hard-hitting' skipper inspires Tigers' second-half 'dominance' - Planet Rugby
content: Ollie Chessum and, inset, Joe Heyes were crucial in Leicester's win over Northampton Following the 28-7 wet-ball win for Leicester against Northampton, here is how we rated Geoff Parling’s Tigers at Welford Road. 15 Freddie Steward: Was among the try scorers when Tigers smashed Saints 41-17 24 weeks ago at home, and he got on the list again with some excellent footwork for his 72nd-minute bonus-point try. Opened his team’s account with a brilliantly struck 19th-minute penalty kick from halfway to punish a Henry Pollock offside; then finished the half by taking exception to how Alex Mitchell interacted with Adam Radwan, igniting the dust-up that fired up Leicester’s second-half dominance. 8 14 Adam Radwan: With Leicester managing a paltry 16 passes compared to 13 first-half kicks in a period dominated by Saints, it was only when he was bundled into touch to end the opening period that you noticed he was playing. His individual duel with George Hendy never materialised until a 70th-minute break from the opposition wing. That resulted in a yellow for Radwan, but it was quickly rescinded after preceding foul play on Solomone Kata was spotted. 5 England latest: Seven bolters Steve Borthwick could select including PREM ace ‘in the form of his life’ 13 Will Wand: A slog of an afternoon in contrast to his illuminating start to the season, this no-frills game seldom invited him to get involved. His alertness remained good, though, and he had no hesitation joining his team’s maul for their opening try four minutes into the second-half. That was excellent team play awareness. 6 12 Solomone Kata: The first of five changes to the Tigers XV following last Sunday’s European loss at Pau, the fit-again midfielder caught the eye with a 23rd-minute catch running backwards following another Fin Smith teaser in behind and a big carry on the lead-up to the second Leicester try for a 13-7 lead. On the receiving end of head contact from carded Saints sub Tom Lockett, which resulted in Radwan getting reprieved for his yellow. 7 11 Gabriel Hamer-Webb: Another recalled player, the Wales pick for November had two fleeting opening-half moments, a 24th-minute aerial duel with Rory Hutchinson and then a super touch finder eight minutes later. Two more moments followed in the second period: his assist for Cameron Henderson’s 52nd-minute try and then his penalty-winning pressure on Tommy Freeman 16 minutes later. 7 10 Billy Searle: Has been at the core of Leicester’s flourish under Parling, but that was a Saturday where silky, ambitious game plans were chucked in the bin. The negative influence of the wet was evident in his flapped attempted catch which gifted Northampton their first try, but he bounced back in the second half, providing solid direction for his hard-working pack. 6 9 Jack van Poortvliet: Back at No.9 with a contract extension also inked, his head-to-head with Mitchell, his England spot rival, would have sparked fireworks on a drier day. Instead, what unfolded was a winter’s game of chess convincingly won in the second half by the Tiger, who greatly helped increase the second-half tempo. Was an important reason why Saints still have not won in Leicester since January 2023. 7 Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. 8 Olly Cracknell: With Leicester struggling for first-half possession, he produced an immense tackle shift to keep them in the contest and prevent them from bleeding on the scoreboard. Was the clear standout eight in contrast to the distracted Pollock. 8 7 Finn Carnduff: Moved across from being at blindside in France last weekend, the England U20 2024 skipper came into his own in Leicester’s second-half surge. Took the lineout catch that set up their lead-taking 44th-minute try and then scored 13 minutes later, crashing through the contact of two Saints tacklers. 8 6 Aaron Wainwright: One of two pack changes along with prop Joe Heyes, Leicester’s second Wales squad pick metaphorically rolled up his sleeves even though Tigers were wearing short-sleeved shirts. Showed his football skills with a left-footed ball stopped with his team attacking on advantage in the play that got them 21-7 up with a penalty. 7 Northampton Saints player ratings: Fin Smith’s ‘standout effort’ in Leicester loss while Henry Pollock avoids ‘shadow-boxing exploits’ 5 Ollie Chessum (c): Plenty of verbals from the skipper to go with plenty of inspired hard-hitting; he was frustrated by a 13th-minute knock-on near the line but was central to denying Saints a try 13 minutes later, a crunching intervention that necessitated a temporary HIA absence. Returned spitting fire and brimstone; his shoving of Pollock up the terrace steps at the interval was pantomime. Excellent second-half, inspiring his team to a 25-0 show of fire. 9 4 Cameron Henderson: Couldn’t get the Leicester lineout going in the first half. For example, lost a 10th-minute lineout jump and while a steal followed 23 minutes later, he was on knocking on at another throw. However, he was a player transformed in the second half and his 52nd-minute try finish was lovely. 8 3 Joe Heyes: It was his 28th-minute scrum penalty win that provided encouragement at another set-piece struggle. That helped to crucially shift the momentum in this area and his joyous second-half outburst of celebration epitomised the feeling of every Leicester fan in the ground with the Saints getting toyed with. 9 2 Jamie Blamire: Mad that his terrible first half at the lineout, where throw after throw went astray, was alleviated by a show of force in the tackle and then the hooker scoring his team’s first try through an early second half maul. A 61st-minute intervention to deny Saints a score was also illuminating. 7 1 Archie van der Flier: Another whose first-half set-piece troubles became second-half celebrations. He also showed up well in the tackle to help earn his team their deserved win. 8 Replacements: Apart from Joaquin Moro being a temporary HIA sub in the first half, Parling didn’t use his bench until the bonus-point win was in the bag – N/A READ MORE: Leicester v Northampton Saints: Five takeaways from East Midlands derby that ‘wrote a few lines’ of England squad as Tigers find key ‘weapon’ © Planet Sport Limited 2026 • All Rights Reserved

title: Barrow v Forest Green Rovers abandoned in 14th minute due to waterlogged pitch - Yahoo Sports
content: The National League match between Barrow and Forest Green Rovers was abandoned in the 14th minute due to a waterlogged pitch and amid farcical scenes. With Storm Boelo and heavy rain hitting the country, the fixture in the north west of England was subject to a "lengthy" pre-match pitch inspection. The match was given the green light to kick off, however, and Barrow quickly took the lead the first minute, but it was immediately clear that the sodden pitch was struggling with the conditions as the ball held up in puddles. It was eventually abandoned by the referee when a back pass from Barrow's Marcel Oakley held up the penalty box, allowing Forest Green's Sean Etaluku to be presented with a goalscoring chance, which he missed. The Barrow X account posted: "Due to circumstances beyond our control, the game has been abandoned." The Forest Green account posted a video of the incident that got the match abandoned, calling it the "deciding factor". The deciding factor....#WeAreFGR💚 pic.twitter.com/hys74INUB8 The club added: "We understand this is very frustrating for the FGR supporters who have travelled to Barrow today. We wish you all safe travels back home." It is a four-hour drive from Forest Green's home stadium to Barrow-in-Furness. At 2:30pm, 30 minutes before kick-off, the Forest Green account posted: "The general consensus at the stadium is that the game will go ahead after the referee's lengthy pitch inspection." The National League South match between Weston-super-Mare and Billericay was also suspended, while in Scotland the League One fixture between Cove Rangers and East Kilbride was also called off.

title: Lecce v Juventus match preview and prediction - Yahoo Sports
content: Juventus travel to Lecce for a must-win match as Luciano Spalletti faces growing pressure to deliver results following the team's recent draw with Rennes in the Europa League. The Bianconeri need to respond positively, with their recent performances raising concerns about their ability to compete consistently across competitions. Juve have performed better in Europe, but their latest result suggests that their poor domestic form is beginning to affect their European campaign as well. The priority now is to stop the rot, restore confidence and ensure their disappointing run does not continue. The Bianconeri have enough quality in their squad to turn things around, and this visit to Lecce offers their players an opportunity to prove they are ready to improve their recent results. However, they must demonstrate greater determination and consistency if they are to return home with all three points. Juve are winless in four of their last five matches, a run that has increased the pressure on Spalletti ahead of this fixture. They now face a Lecce side that secured an impressive 3-0 away victory against Udinese in their previous match. That result will give the hosts plenty of confidence before this encounter. Playing in front of their own supporters, Lecce will believe they can trouble Spalletti's men and take advantage of any uncertainty in the Juventus performance. Juventus have struggled to deliver in matches they are expected to win, and their recent performances suggest the team still has significant problems to address. Spalletti will need his players to show greater focus and composure if they are to avoid another disappointing result. The involvement of Randal Kolo Muani and Nick Woltemade has not yet solved Juventus' wider problems. Despite their presence in the starting line-up, the team have continued to struggle for consistency, leaving questions about their ability to turn individual quality into convincing performances. Lecce will be encouraged by those difficulties and will hope to make life uncomfortable for the visitors. Their recent victory against Udinese provides a timely boost, and they have the opportunity to test Juventus' confidence from the opening minutes. However, the historical record favours the Bianconeri. Lecce have failed to win any of their last ten matches against Juventus, who have claimed victory in seven of those encounters. That record offers encouragement to Spalletti's side despite their recent struggles. Juventus must still produce a much improved performance, but we expect them to overcome Lecce and secure another important victory.

title: Liverpool v Brighton & Hove Albion: Team news - Liverpool FC
content:
Bradley Barcola is fit to face Brighton & Hove Albion but Liverpool will be without Dominik Szoboszlai and Victor Munoz may also be absent. The Reds' busy schedule continues on Sunday, when the Seagulls visit Anfield for a 2pm GMT kick-off in the Premier League. Barcola did not take part in team training on Thursday but, 24 hours later, Andoni Iraola allayed any concerns about the forward's availability. "Bradley has trained today normally. He's fine with no problem," the head coach said, during his pre-match press conference on Friday afternoon. "It was just a matter of sometimes you have to deal with the loads and we consider sometimes they have to stay inside. But he's fine." Szoboszlai and Munoz both sustained injuries during last weekend's win at Brentford and subsequently missed the midweek victory over Villarreal. And when asked about their fitness, Iraola replied: "Victor, he has the knock he received against Brentford [in the] first half. He could finish the game very well. "But he's dealing with some pain since then and it was too early the other day against Villarreal. I don't know if he's going to arrive. I think it's going to be difficult but I really don't know. "Dom is going to be out this weekend. I don't think he's far but he hasn't trained with the group still. And also considering the other day [against Brentford] that we started him and he had to go out, we will probably take one or two days more than we would last week. “He's in a good place. Dom is already training outside alone and is going to train with the group, but he's not ready for this one." Ryan Gravenberch is eligible for selection after serving a one-match suspension in the Premier League, while Liverpool's three long-term absentees – Conor Bradley, Hugo Ekitike and Giovanni Leoni – remain sidelined. Sunday's game is the fifth of nine in a 28-day spell for Iraola's side across three different competitions. "We are changing a lot the team because we are playing basically every three or four days," he added. "So, sometimes the players are tired or there is more risk involved and we are deciding to give more rest or to use more fresh legs when we decide – and it's going to continue to be the same against Brighton, Chelsea and Arsenal because this doesn't stop. "So, we have to continue and I'm happy because we are kind of changing a little bit the team, giving some rest and I think overall they are answering well, the players." Brighton's Yankuba Minteh and Mats Wieffer are closing in on returns from injury, and could be available this Sunday. Minteh has been out with his issue since pre-season, while Wieffer injured his knee at the end of August. "There is an option. Especially with Minteh, there might be an option. But definitely next week," Seagulls head coach Fabian Hurzeler said on Friday. "They will train tomorrow with the team and then we will see if they are available or not. "If they are not available for his game then I am quite convinced we will see them back in the squad next week for the [Manchester] City games." Pascal Struijk has sat out their past two matches – with Crystal Palace and FK Jablonec – and will continue to be monitored. "It is not a big issue but it is something that can get bigger if you risk it too early," added Hurzeler. "We have so many games and we have to take care of the health of the players. We have to make wise decisions." Diego Gomez and Maxim De Cuyper were rested against Jablonec on Thursday, with goalkeeper Jason Steele missing the match in Czechia due to illness. The visitors look set to remain without Femi Azeez, Evan Ferguson, Kaoru Mitoma, Stefanos Tzimas and Zadok Yohanna. title: We Tested Chevy’s New Small-Block V-8 to Find Out How Much It Improves the Corvette’s Performance - Car and Driver
content:
With the Z51 package and the new LS6 6.7-liter V-8 under the hood, how does the updated Stingray compare with the old one? Welcome to Car and Driver's Testing Hub, where we zoom in on the test numbers. We've been pushing vehicles to their limits since 1956 to provide objective data to bolster our subjective impressions (you can see how we test here). It should come as no surprise that the 2027 Chevy Corvette Stingray is a performance monster. Every C8 Corvette—hell, just about every Corvette—punches above its weight class in terms of performance, but with the launch of Chevy’s new LS6 small-block V-8, the Stingray is officially a 200-mph car for less than $75,000. Now that we’ve tested the 2027 Stingray, we figured it was worth comparing how the new version stacks up against the old one. Given that our example was the entry-level 1LT trim level, we figured the fairest comparison would be to look at the last 1LT Stingray we tested, which was all the way back in 2020 (the mid-engine C8’s first model year). See all results for new 2027 Chevrolet Corvette Stingray / Grand Sport for sale and new 2026 Chevrolet Corvette Stingray / Grand Sport for sale near 23917 As anticipated, the new Stingray is quicker, though not by much. Our tester came equipped with the $5395 Z51 Performance package, which adds Michelin Pilot Sport S5 summer tires, stiffer springs, better cooling, an electronically controlled limited-slip differential, and considerably larger brakes. Add it all together, and the sprint to 60 mph arrives in a mere 2.7 seconds. That’s incredibly quick, but not much quicker than the 2020 car’s 2.8-second run. Keep your foot in it, though, and the gap widens a bit. The new car hits 100 mph in 6.9 seconds and 150 mph in 18.6 ticks. The previous Z51 required an additional three-tenths to break into the triple digits, and it cracked 150 mph as the stopwatch read 19.4 seconds. The 2027 is quicker through the quarter mile too, rushing through in 11.0 seconds flat at 124 mph vs. the 2020 car’s 11.2-second run at 122 mph. While the base Stingray is good for an even 200 mph, adding the Z51 package actually dials that figure back to 183 mph—one mph lower than the previous Z51. The top-speed penalty comes from a combination of larger cooling ducts for the brakes, the added drag from the front splitter and rear wing, and, perhaps most importantly, a shorter 5.56:1 final-drive ratio (same as in the Z06), which hampers its overall top speed. On the one hand, the Z51 package limits top speed. On the other hand, it makes up for it in the braking department. Stopping from 70 mph happens in just 149 feet for both the new and old Stingrays. When stopping from 100 mph, the newer car took 297 feet, versus the older car’s 301 feet, basically a dead heat. See all results for new 2027 Chevrolet Corvette Stingray / Grand Sport for sale and new 2026 Chevrolet Corvette Stingray / Grand Sport for sale near 23917 Both cars wore 245-series front and 305-series rear Michelin Pilot Sport S tires, while the 2020 car wore the 4S and the ’27 gets the newer S5 rubber. title: Hull City v Brentford: Key stats and talking points - Yahoo Sports
content: Hull City face Brentford for the first time in a top-flight fixture. BBC Sport examines some of the key themes going into their meeting at MKM Stadium on Sunday. Hull find themselves in the paradoxical situation of having made a strong start to the season despite failing to win any of their past five matches. That run has included draws with both Chelsea and Everton after falling behind, while history suggests that Hull's tally of nine points after seven matches offers an excellent chance of Premier League survival. Of the 13 promoted teams to have amassed exactly nine points at this stage, only five went on to be relegated. The most recent of those was Norwich City in 2015-16. The bedrock of Hull's early promise has been an unbeaten start at home, with a win and two draws so far. Across the past 11 seasons, the only two promoted teams to remain undefeated in their first four home games were Wolves in 2018-19 and Sunderland last season. They both went on to finish in seventh. The Tigers' success so far, both home and away, has been built on picking the right moment to go after opposing teams. They rank just 15th in the Premier League for high turnovers (defined as winning the ball within 40 metres of your opponent's goal), yet only three teams have recorded more shots that have originated from a high turnover. In other words, Hull City are selective as to when they press but often do so effectively in dangerous areas. Hull next face a Brentford side who have conceded more high turnovers than any Premier League side other than Aston Villa; an unwelcome statistic for a visiting team with an unwelcome habit of throwing away points this season. Two red cards were reasonable mitigation for Brentford's 2-1 loss to Liverpool last weekend, a game in which they took the lead through Keane Lewis-Potter. It means that Brentford have now dropped an unrivalled 11 points from winning positions in 2026-27. If ill-discipline and late goals have both been factors in Brentford's failure to see out games, so too has been the form of forward Igor Thiago. The Brazil international was a vital part of their success last season and scored 22 goals, but he has managed just one in seven outings so far this season, despite an expected goals total of 3.69 - compromising Brentford's ability to kill off matches. Thiago, though, can take confidence from his record against promoted clubs, scoring six goals in his past six Premier League appearances against them. If Thiago's form was to improve this weekend, it could end a curious hoodoo for the Bees: they have not won a top-flight match in Yorkshire since 1947, drawing four and losing one of their five visits in the Premier League.

title: The datacentre next door: on the frontline of tech’s latest David v Goliath battle - The Guardian
content: The AI boom is pitting local residents against corporate giants seeking to power their energy-hungry networks – but one Welsh city is fighting back Dale Johnston opens the gate to his neat suburban garden on the western fringes of Newport in South Wales. There’s a trampoline and a slide on the lawn for his grandchildren, and chairs for him and his wife. He should be enjoying the light draining from the perfect autumnal sky – but almost his entire view is blotted out by a vast expanse of prefabricated panels. The 23 metre-high grey hulk looming over him and his neighbours is a hyperscale datacentre. It is heralded by the area’s Labour politicians as a job creator, yet all Johnston can think about is what he has lost: “Before, the sun used to come around here and it was lovely.” The way residents have been treated is “disgusting”. Johnston, who used to work for a chemical company in the city, worries what their lives will be like when the centre is switched on: the 36 sets of air blast coolers, needed to stop the chips inside overheating, most likely generate a constant drone, while regular testing of 60 back-up diesel generators, to prevent costly interruption to the flow of data, could produce harmful fumes. He already has to keep his bathroom window closed to stop the low hum from another facility on the rapidly expanding 46-acre datacentre campus that borders the small enclave of 27 houses. His wife, a nurse who works night shifts, can barely sleep already. He shakes his head in despair: “We just don’t know what’s going to happen.” Johnston can talk about little else, but he feels no one in authority is listening. He’s invited councillors and MPs backing the development to visit his garden. But “they won’t come around here to see what they’ve done”. This is the frontline of Britain’s datacentre boom, which is pitting residents against giant US tech firms seeking to build a network of facilities capable of providing the immense computing muscle for powerful AI models. There are 315 hyperscale datacentres waiting to connect to the national grid, which carries electricity from power plants to homes and businesses (hyperscale typically means facilities with at least 5,000 servers and 10,000 sq ft in size). Combined, these new centres will require 73GW of power, 28GW higher than the typical peak energy demand of 45GW on a cold winter’s day. Wales is one of the main development hotspots outside London. It already has the largest datacentre capacity beyond the capital, with new hyperscale facilities planned for former industrial and urban sites. The Keir Starmer-led Labour government viewed this as an inevitable revolution, which the country must embrace or be left behind. It established five AI growth zones to push more datacentres through the planning system and speed up connections to the national grid. The new prime minister, Andy Burnham, has signalled little will change, turning down calls for a moratorium and insisting datacentres bring economic benefits. But anti-datacentre groups springing up in villages, towns and cities across the country see it rather differently: as the imposition of a resource-hungry, polluting industry that increases profits for often US big tech, with little tangible benefit to local people or the country as a whole. Digital storage is nothing new. The first home PC users saved files on floppy discs and hard drives; businesses used their own server rooms in the 80s and 90s, then moved to off-site facilities as their needs grew. But the development of cloud computing services in the 2010s, such as Google Drive, and AI chatbots in the 2020s, like ChatGPT, led to even greater information and processing demands, which the tech industry insists can only be met by larger and larger datacentres. This has driven huge speculative bets on hyperscale hubs, which investors and tech firms hope will one day reap the rewards of an AI-led transformation of the economy. Globally, it is estimated spending on new facilities could reach $7tn by 2030 – more than double the cost of the New Deal, the Marshall Plan to rebuild Europe after the second world war and the Apollo space programme combined, even allowing for inflation. The US is at the forefront of the boom, already hosting roughly half of the world’s hyperscale capacity. But the industry is facing a furious backlash, with three- quarters of Americans now opposed to datacentre development and blaming it for increasing energy bills, threatening water supplies in drought-hit areas and spewing out toxic fumes. More than 500 counties and municipalities have passed permanent or temporary datacentre bans. Loudoun County in northern Virginia sits in what is known as Data Center Alley because it is home to more facilities than anywhere else in the world. Greg Pirio’s life was turned upside down when a gas-powered datacentre opened 150 metres from his home last year. “This neighbourhood was calm and peaceful, and it’s turned into this nightmare,” he says on a video call. “Our quality of life has been degraded so much.” The noise from the centre’s eight gas turbines is “like being at an airport with all these engines roaring,” Pirio says. “It has given many of my neighbours headaches. It has kept children up at night.” Pirio, who used to work for the Voice of America radio station, has also developed health problems since it opened, including dry eyes and chest tightness. Once he had to leave his house because he was struggling to breathe: “I know whenever the diesel generators are on, because I feel it in my lungs.” The UK has not yet seen the same level of opposition as the US. But anti-datacentre groups are gathering momentum. Residents in east London are waging a high-profile campaign against a new datacentre on Brick Lane, including protesting outside the offices of Angela Rayner, the communities secretary, who overturned a council decision blocking the scheme. Seasoned campaigner Owen Espley, who works for environmental charity Global Action Plan, is helping scores of residents’ groups organise against planned datacentres. “This summer has been wild. Every other week a new group has popped up. Petitions are getting thousands of signatures in days,” he says. “Communities are in uproar, and most politicians are playing catch-up.” Espley has been taken aback by the gulf between the government’s conviction that there is no alternative and ordinary people’s deepening understanding of the complex issues at stake. “There has been a real grassroots questioning of datacentres that connects British Bangladeshis in Brick Lane with Hertfordshire villagers and communities in Northumberland, who want good jobs to come back,” he says. “It is astounding.” In fact, there are many alternative pathways to market-­led expansion – from tougher regulation to prioritising publicly-owned data infrastructure – which serve communal goals, such as the heart disease and dementia research powered by Bristol University’s new Isambard-AI facility. “First, we need strong standards for private datacentres,” Espley says. “Second, we need industrial strategy to deliver our own public computer, rather than an assumption that US big tech building and owning everything is the only way forward.” On the deprived eastern edges of Cardiff, the early morning sunshine is warming a car park dotted with scraggly weeds. The perimeter fence is overgrown with brambles, with patches of singed, blackened grass from a recent wildfire visible just beyond. It looks abandoned but soon cars carrying doctors, nurses and other NHS staff start arriving. They are here to catch free buses to Cardiff’s Heath hospital, the largest in Wales. Hundreds are said to use the park and ride every day, but it is under threat because Labour-controlled Cardiff council wants to sell the land to a property developer, Curtis Hall, to build a hyperscale data facility. The centre will use up to 150 megawatts (MW) of electricity a year, more than triple the demand of a city the size of Cardiff. The development is one of the most controversial in Wales. Council meetings have been disrupted and more than 1,200 planning objections lodged. Last month, the new Plaid Cymru-led government ordered the council to put the application on hold while it considered whether to take the decision out of councillors’ hands. Campaigners are determined to keep up the pressure on the Welsh government. Sue Elias, a retired librarian with seemingly endless reserves of energy, dashes back and forth reattaching her “Ditch the datacentre” banner to the car park fence and taping leaflets to the bus stop glass. “What is going to happen to all the people who use the park and ride? It’s bonkers,” she says. Elias has leafleted the park and ride every Wednesday morning for six weeks. Today she is collecting signatures for an open letter to prove it is well used – so far she has added the names of 1,300 staff and patients. “I’ve not done anything like this before but I’m told I’m a natural,” she says with a mischievous smile, before breaking off to speak to staff arriving for the next bus. She belongs to community-based union Acorn, which has campaigned against the scheme, and has taken part in protests, including bursting into a council planning meeting in July. “We’d sent emails, done petitions, but we’d had nothing back – tumbleweed. They’re our elected representatives … They should be talking with us.” It is hard to find anyone in support of the plan in the queue for the bus, which runs three times an hour. “I use it every day. Without it, I probably wouldn’t continue working at the hospital,” says Ami George, a midwife. “Parking there causes that much stress.” Across Cardiff’s Rhymney River, which curves around the proposed datacentre development, the area’s newest residents have only recently moved into 100 homes built under the city council’s flagship house-building programme. Nick Richards, a freelance filmmaker and skateboarder, and his wife arrived in November. “It felt like the stars had aligned because there is a brand new skate park up the road … the best in Cardiff. It’s amazing,” he says. “I never pictured myself living in suburbia but when we came we saw kids playing outside and thought, this is a really nice area.” Like many other residents on the estate, Richards had no idea the council was planning to sell the park and ride to a datacentre developer. They moved in two months before the planning application was submitted. Instead of enjoying their new life, they now fear they will never be able to sell. Their home is 300 metres from what the plans describe as the temporary energy centre, which includes seven giant gas turbines. They are expected to power the facility around the clock for five years, according to documents filed by the developer. “I feel trapped,” Richards says, pacing his kitchen. “I couldn’t look prospective buyers in the eye and not say there’s going to be seven gas turbines right next to them.” Richards has pored over the planning documents and leafleted every house on the new estate, including a care home, which will be just 150 metres from the turbines. “This datacentre will be powered by gas turbines,” he says. “They will pump nitrogen dioxide into our atmosphere. There will also be fine particulate matter and formaldehyde. All these toxins cause health conditions, such as asthma, COPD and heart disease.” Air quality assessments commissioned by the developer estimate the emissions will be within safe levels. Curtis Hall says the scheme cannot proceed without 100% compliance with all environmental and public health regulatory requirements. There are more than 100 other planned UK datacentres aiming to use gas turbines due to the long wait to be connected to the grid. Richards doesn’t want his estate to be a test case. “Within a mile of this datacentre are 30,000 people. But the people building this centre don’t live here ... They don’t give two shits about Welsh people.” A stone’s throw away is Llanrumney Hall, once the home of privateer and slave trader Sir Henry Morgan, who gave his name to Captain Morgan rum. It is now a thriving community centre, with a cafe, recording studio and creche. Labour councillor Lee Bridgeman is vaping on an outdoor table, dressed in a hoodie and baseball cap. He ran the local youth centre until it was lost to austerity-era cuts, and though he’s a high-ranking councillor, jointly responsible for housing and communities, he does regular youth work shifts in the area, one of the poorest in Cardiff. “Llanrumney runs through my veins,” he says. “I’m not your usual politician. I don’t go to conferences. I got into politics to help the community.” Bridgeman is charming and friendly – but he is not afraid of a fight. He is one of the few public figures in the area who has spoken out in support of the development, sometimes clashing with anti-datacentre campaigners on local Facebook groups. “Some of the information being spread is scaremongering,” he says. “They are telling residents their electricity bills will go up … the river and reservoir will be drained … It’s false information.” Many of these fears stem from the US, where the rapid expansion of hyperscale facilities has been linked to rising electricity bills, water shortages and toxic air pollution. Bridgeman argues that “planning processes are totally different in the UK. So whereas [US authorities] turn a blind eye to some of the environmental impacts of those monstrosities, that would never happen in the UK.” He “wouldn’t be comfortable” if the gas turbines were running for five years but thinks they might not be needed if the datacentre can connect to the grid sooner. The backlash has caught him by surprise, but he blames outside activists. “I didn’t see it coming. I didn’t think there would be this much interference,” he says. Emotions are running high in the city. Some residents say they have been blocked by councillors when trying to question them on Facebook. Planning committee members have received threatening emails, Bridgeman says. “Threats like ‘I will come after you ... we will make your life hell.’ That shouldn’t happen.” Although the datacentre will employ only up to 125 people when it is built, Bridgeman believes it could encourage other big companies to east Cardiff: “I’m told the knock-on effect could lead to thousands of jobs.” Later that day, residents squeeze into the local boxing club for a public meeting about the datacentre plan. It is standing room only, with people lining the walls. Bridgeman repeats his claim that few locals have complained: “I have hundreds of emails from residents ... So far I’ve had two emails with regards to the datacentre.” Some in the audience react angrily. There are shouts of, “We don’t know you, that’s why” and, “Have you heard of social media?” One woman stands up and says, “Don’t tell me you haven’t been privy to the meetings … or things online.” In a show of hands, roughly three-quarters of the 80 to 100 people in the room indicate they are from Llanrumney, almost all opposed. There are cries of, “There you are … you don’t need emails!” and, “That’s every person!” Almost three weeks later, Bridgeman performs a sudden about-turn, submitting a formal letter of objection to the scheme, noting that he has heard from a large number of residents. The UK hyperscale buildout has been focused on London, but datacentre developers are increasingly targeting areas outside the south-east, to escape severe electrical grid capacity limits. Wales already has the largest datacentre capacity of anywhere outside the capital. Many more could be coming: five of Wales’s largest new and proposed datacentres will consume more electricity than all Welsh homes put together. While the previous Welsh Labour administration welcomed the building spree, claiming giant tech firms’ investment would generate thousands of jobs, the Plaid Cymru-led government has been more circumspect, with ministers emphasising it must benefit Wales. In the light and airy Welsh parliament building, which overlooks Cardiff Bay, opposition is growing. Plaid Cymru’s Nick Carter, who is the Senedd member for Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf, which includes Cardiff East, worries that the surging market will benefit developers and US tech firms rather than the public. “As a party, we’re not going to want to see a proliferation of datacentres, haphazardly being built across the country, on what may be an opportunistic basis,” he says. Carter, who has a background in commercial property, has examined the Cardiff plans in detail. He says the developer, Curtis Hall, has no track record in datacentres; “They could be a front for someone else: Google, Microsoft, whoever. I can understand why these operators need datacentres, but I’m not sure members of the public share the need.” In response, Curtis Hall says it never claimed it would operate the facility itself, adding it had been working on datacentre projects for five years. Carter is glad the Welsh government has intervened in Cardiff. But he doesn’t believe Wales needs to follow Scotland by imposing a moratorium on new datacentres: “The Welsh government is developing a strategy for datacentres nationally. We’ll see what comes out of that.” However, it is not clear how the Welsh government can meet its goal to reach net zero by 2040 without limiting datacentre expansion. Carter admits, “It’s massively problematic.” In Westminster, similar questions have been asked. The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology tells me the government will enable the development of datacentres by generating unprecedented amounts of clean power. A soft autumnal dusk descends on the residents living beside the new datacentre in Newport. Its sleek industrial-grey walls cast shadows across the closest gardens and homes. Much of the anger and frustration that met the original proposals has given way to weariness and resignation. Some residents talk of moving away, while others are mollified by meetings with the US-based data campus operator, Vantage. Yet their troubles may only just be beginning – right now, only one of the three Vantage datacentres is operational. Microsoft will be opening its own nearby soon. When all are running, there could be upwards of 500 air handling units working at the same time, with back-up diesel generators needing regular testing, so they can immediately fire up if there is a power cut. Newport council’s chief scientific officer warned during the planning process that the fumes from all the generators had the “potential to cause unacceptable air pollution levels under use, and testing needs to be understood and mitigation proposed, if needed”. The council tells me it doesn’t have a duty to monitor emissions from generators, but says its officers check air quality management plans, and ask managers to minimise the impact of generator tests. Vantage says all its facilities operate in accordance with noise and air quality controls. It says it will monitor impacts and investigate concerns when the new centre opens. Some residents have already given up on democratic process. Johnston fought the proposals through the planning process but felt he was ignored. “We’ve been let down by all of them. I’ve had electoral roll cards come through my door. But I’m voting for none of them … I can’t trust them. They don’t care about any of us.” Over the road are older homes, where staff working on a nearby wealthy estate once lived. Sonia Thomas, a retired teacher, has lived in the same housekeeper’s cottage since 1969. She can remember when orchards and fields fanned out in front of their gardens but now she doesn’t even know if the sun is shining. “From inside you see grey, not blue,” she says, glancing at the datacentre filling the sky. “It’s horrible.”

The words of Como 1907 head coach Cesc Fàbregas ahead of Como 1907-Sassuolo: "I think the team is still a work in progress, but I’m sure we’ll get to where we want to be, step by step. What allows you to achieve your goals over the course of a season is the atmosphere you create, the way the team plays, how it responds in the toughest moments and how it behaves when everything is going well. We’re building a very specific culture and way of working here in Mozzate, day by day, with the aim of becoming a consistent team in everything we do and everything we want to be. I really like Alberto as a coach, his ideas and his courage. Above all, his teams play football. He has grown tremendously as a coach. Sassuolo are a well-built team with plenty of options and some very good players, including young talents. I enjoy watching them during the season because there’s always something to learn from them." Now in its 13th Serie A season out of the last 14, Sassuolo has consistently established itself in the top flight thanks to a winning club culture. Through scouting, developing, and promoting young players—often Italians—the Neroverdi have earned acclaim and success, maintaining a sustainable model despite the turnover of coaches and players over the years. Historically, Sassuolo has relied on the 4-3-3 formation as its cornerstone, and Aquilani—in his first season with the Neroverdi—also favors this tactical setup, fielding several young, up-and-coming players alongside a few veterans to provide leadership and experience. Sassuolo’s iconic player is undoubtedly Berardi, the club’s all-time leading scorer with 132 goals in Serie A, who could also become the club’s all-time record appearance holder in the top flight. The Neroverdi’s number 10 plays as a right winger as usual, while on the opposite flank, Laurienté provides dribbling flair and speed. Esposito and Bowie round out the attack, sharing minutes in the center. Sassuolo’s strength, however, also lies in midfield, where the experienced Matić serves as the team’s anchor and stabilizing force. Alongside him, Bacola, Thorstvedt, and Adzic rotate in midfield; Adzic is the Neroverdi’s leading scorer so far this season with 3 goals. Central defender Odenthal, a former player for Como, has scored 2 goals, as has Van der Brempt. Both started in Sassuolo’s last match, with Ćaleta-Car and Doig rounding out the back four protecting Murić’s goal. Historically, Como 1907 and Sassuolo faced off for the first time in league play only last season, with each team claiming one victory. The BiancoBlu secured a 2-0 win on November 28 at the Sinigaglia, thanks to goals by Tasos Douvikas and Alberto Moreno. However, their very first meeting took place on September 24, 2025, in Coppa Italia, also at the Sinigaglia. In that match, the Lariani won 3-0 courtesy of a brace by Jesus Rodriguez and a goal by Tasos Douvikas.

title: Smith vs Puello: Fight predictions from boxing world including Chantelle Cameron, Tony Bellew & Paulie Malignaggi - BBC
content: WBC light-welterweight champion Dalton Smith (left) has won all 19 pro fights with 14 stoppages Dalton Smith will make the first defence of his WBC light-welterweight title on home soil when he faces former champion Alberto Puello in Sheffield on Saturday. Unbeaten Smith, 29, returns to the ring for the first time since becoming world champion with a stunning knockout of Subriel Matias in New York in January. Dominican Republic fighter Puello, 32, is aiming to become a three-time world champion, having lost his WBC belt to Matias on points last year. Smith will have the backing of his home crowd at the Utilita Arena. Can he keep his dream of fighting at Sheffield Wednesday's Hillsborough stadium alive with another win? Or will the tricky and experienced southpaw Puello, who has lost just once in 26 professional fights, ruin the homecoming? BBC Sport spoke to figures from across the boxing world to get their predictions on who will come out on top. How world champion Smith can become a mainstream star "I think it's going to be a great fight, I think there will be a lot of close rounds, but I'm going for a majority decision win for Smith in a really tough fight." "What a brilliant fight this is. It's such a terrific match-up with contrasting styles. You have a slick southpaw in Puello and the tough, rugged, well-schooled Smith. Puello being a southpaw will suit Dalton who throws a fantastic right hand. "This is fine margins - high-level chess. I think Dalton will come through via decision, or perhaps a late stoppage, and he will have produced two back-to-back victories to cement his place in the top 15 pound-for-pound rankings." "I think this will be an interesting fight. Both guys have a similar sort of style. Puello is a boxer-puncher who goes really well to the body. He throws that loopy left hand shot quite well that Dalton will have to be quite careful of. "It will be cagey at the start and I think Puello will fall behind a little bit. Dalton is a better boxer than him and better at his game. Puello will then have to come forward and I think that will suit Dalton. "So I see Dalton winning quite a wide points decision." "It's a good fight and I think Puello is a good fighter but I'm Team Smith. He boxes well and his style has matured. Puello has fast hands and is good in close but Smith can find a way to beat him. If he knocks him out then it's a big statement, but I'll go for a Smith win on points." "This is a harder fight for Smith than Matias. Matias was a monster, while Puello is a clever boxer who sits on the back foot and punches nice and long. He's southpaw which makes it awkward to adjust your feet and stance. "Ultimately, I think the angles of attack will be the difference for Smith. I think it might be a bit of a frustrating night for him but I think he comes out on top on points. "It will be relatively entertaining - not as exciting as the win over Matias, perhaps - but a good homecoming for the champion." "I'm backing Dalton, he's been my guy since we were 12 years old. He was my roomate at every tournament and now is his time as WBC world champion." "I'm backing Dalton Smith to beat Alberto Puello and retain his world title. Smith's power, accuracy and impressive stoppage win over Subriel Matias make him a dangerous opponent. "Although Puello's experience and awkward southpaw style could make it a tough fight, I think Smith's power and work-rate will prove too much. Smith to win by unanimous decision." "Puello can be awkward and disrupt rhythm as he did in wins over guys like now WBA champion Gary Antuanne Russell, but Dalton's a big light-welterweight and his boxing is on point as well as intelligent decision-making. "His stoppage win over Subriel Matias was impressive but I see Dalton winning this one on points.  Puello will complicate things in some moments, but Smith wins a comfortable decision." "It's a big fight. I think the Utilita Arena - pound-for-pound - is the noisiest venue in the country. To use a football analogy, I think it will have to be a 12th man for Dalton. "I think he's up against it. Puello is a very special talent, as is Dalton who put on a performance of a lifetime in January. "Dalton has a lot of the advantages but Puello comes here with experience at the highest level at this division. He wants the belt back, which he thinks was robbed from him in his loss to Matias. "I do edge towards the current champion because of home advantage, but I wouldn't be shocked if Puello walks away with the belt." "Dalton is a real hero in Sheffield but Puello is very dangerous. He's a southpaw and a former two-time world champion. "It's a very tough first defence but Dalton has home advantage, the age and the unbeaten record. He probably has plans A, B, C and D. He's a very clever boxer whose background has been perfect - an excellent amateur and a solid professional." "I think Dalton will stop him late on - round nine or 10. Dalton is just too good for Puello, he'll try to put pressure on but Dalton will just have his number." "Dalton will have a little bit too much speed and a little bit too much flair. The one thing that Dalton has to watch out for is he cannot afford to slow it down to Puello's pace. He's decent with his jab, he likes his opponent to stand in front, he doesn't like it when they move. "If Dalton is in and out with his feet, plays it tricky, he'll be able to beat him fairly comfortably as long as he doesn't stand and trade." "I've got Dalton winning on points. I think it will be a competitive fight but Dalton will edge it." Notifications, social media and more with BBC Sport The candid meeting that 'changed' Spurs - are they finally on way back? title: Cadillac Celebrates Its 125th Birthday with a Limited Run of V-8-Powered Escalades That Each Cost $239K - Car and Driver
content: The 125th Anniversary Collector Series honors Cadillac’s history by dressing a limited run of Escalade-Vs in special-edition attire. In the early 1900s, the Wright brothers were experimenting with flight, Henry Ford was developing the Model T, and Albert Einstein was making finishing touches to his theory of relativity. At the same time, Cadillac was emerging with the 1903 Runabout, which made 10 horsepower from a single-cylinder engine and cost $850—about $33,300 in today’s economy. Next year will mark 125 years since Cadillac’s founding, and a lot has changed since the Runabout’s release. To celebrate the luxury brand’s milestone anniversary, Cadillac is releasing the 2027 Escalade-V 125th Anniversary Collector Series, which will have a very limited production run. See all results for new 2027 Cadillac Escalade / Escalade ESV for sale near 23917 The Anniversary Collector Series is all about exclusivity. While buyers can’t choose much beyond the exterior paint color in terms of the vehicle’s appearance, they can add a bit of personalization by selecting their own VIN and serial number. To complement the Midnight Stone Frost or Vibrant White Tricoat paint, the Escalade-V 125th Anniversary wears forged 24-inch wheels and features blue brake calipers, dark-finish badges, puddle lamps with heritage V-8 graphics, and carbon-fiber details on the grille surround, lower rear fascia, mirror caps, and engine cover. This special edition doesn’t change much under the hood, but the Escalade-V is plenty powerful as-is. A supercharged 6.2-liter V-8 makes 682 horsepower to cart the massive SUV to 60 mph in just 4.3 seconds in our testing. Inside, Santorini Blue stitching and seatbelts connect Cadillac’s racing history with the special-edition Escalade-V. The blue accents pair with a sleek black-and-gray interior, Collector Series floormats, exclusive interior badging, and a blue key fob. The Escalade-V 125th Anniversary Collector Series will be limited to 252 units and sold only in the United States and Canada. Orders are open now, with pricing starting at around $239,000.
